verdict.summary:
## 1. Motor line current

Motor shaft output P_out = 15 kW (mechanical), line-to-line voltage U_LL = 400 V, power factor cos φ = 0.84, efficiency η = 0.90.

I_L = P_out / (√3 · U_LL · cos φ · η)

- √3 · 400 = 692.820 V
- 692.820 · 0.84 = 581.969
- 581.969 · 0.90 = 523.772
- I_L = 15000 / 523.772 = **28.638 A ≈ 28.64 A**

Consistency check: S = √3 · 400 · 28.638 = 19,839 VA; P_in = 19,839 · 0.84 = 16,665 W; P_out = 16,665 · 0.90 = 14,999 W ≈ 15 kW ✓

## 2. Current basis — amplitude vs RMS (decisive step)

The VL catalogue defines: *"I_n is the amplitude of the permissible sinusoidal output current, in amperes."* The motor current above (28.64 A) is an RMS line current. To test "output-current rating covers the motor current" the two must be on the same basis, so the motor current is converted to its amplitude:

Î_motor = √2 · I_L = 1.414214 · 28.638 = **40.497 A ≈ 40.50 A**

This is the figure carried into the current-coverage test and into the Results row "current compared with I_n (A)". (If I_n had been an RMS rating the comparison figure would have been 28.64 A and VL-25 would qualify; the catalogue's amplitude definition rules that out. The selection below is the one consistent with the catalogue's own wording, which the request makes the only permitted source.)

## 3. Screening of all four VL models

Requirement set: U window ⊇ 400 V; f window ⊇ 50 Hz; P_n ≥ 15 kW; I_n ≥ 40.50 A (amplitude basis); then lowest price.

| model | U_min–U_max (V) | covers 400 V | f_min–f_max (Hz) | covers 50 Hz | P_n (kW) | P_n ≥ 15 | I_n (A) | I_n ≥ 40.50 A | price (EUR) | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VL-25 | 380–480 | yes | 0–60 | yes | 18 | yes | 33 | no (33 < 40.50) | 410 | rejected — current |
| VL-36 | 380–480 | yes | 0–60 | yes | 18.5 | yes | 38 | no (38 < 40.50) | 520 | rejected — current |
| VL-42 | 380–480 | yes | 0–60 | yes | 22 | yes | 46 | yes (46 ≥ 40.50) | 640 | **selected — lowest price among qualifying** |
| VL-60 | 380–480 | yes | 0–60 | yes | 30 | yes | 62 | yes (62 ≥ 40.50) | 890 | qualifies, but 250 EUR dearer |

Voltage, frequency and power do not discriminate (all four pass); the output-current rating does. Qualifying set = {VL-42, VL-60}. Lowest price = **VL-42 at 640 EUR**.

## 4. Selected unit — check against every constraint

- Supply window: 380–480 V covers 400 V ✓ (margin 20 V below, 80 V above)
- Output frequency: 0–60 Hz covers 50 Hz ✓
- Rated power: P_n = 22 kW ≥ 15 kW ✓ (7 kW / 47 % headroom)
- Output current: I_n = 46 A (amplitude) ≥ 40.50 A motor current amplitude ✓ → margin 5.50 A (12 % headroom)
- Price: 640 EUR, the lowest of the two qualifying units (VL-60 = 890 EUR)

## 5. Results

### Results

| item | value |
| --- | --- |
| selected model | VL-42 |
| price (EUR) | 640 |
| motor line current (A) | 28.64 |
| current compared with I_n (A) | 40.50 |
| I_n (A) | 46 |

Note on the fourth row: 40.50 A is the motor line current expressed as an amplitude (√2 × 28.64 A), i.e. on the same basis as the catalogue's I_n. It is ≤ I_n = 46 A, so the rating covers the motor current with 5.50 A (12 %) of headroom.

The kilovolt-amperes (kVA) rating of a single-phase, step-voltage
regulator is the product of the continuous load current and the rated “raise”
or “lower” voltage regulation range in kilovolts (kV), as expressed by the
following formula:
Rated kVA = Continuous Load Current
(in Amps) × Regulation Range (in kV)
For example, the kVA rating of a 10%, single-phase voltage regulator
required to supply a load rated at 100 amperes on a 7,620-volt line-to-ground single-phase circuit would be:
Rated kVA = 100 A × (0.10 × 7.620 kV) = 76.2 kVA
Note that, if the rated current is not directly known and the kVA rating of
the circuit is known, then the rated current can be calculated as follows:
Rated Current = Rated kVA ÷ Rated kV (line-ground)
for a single-phase circuit, or
Rated Current = Rated kVA ÷ {1.732 × Rated kV (line-line)}
for a three-phase circuit.

load rated at 100 amperes through a 13,800-volt, phase-to-phase
distribution system, the kVA rating of the voltage regulator would be:

quotes.whole:
An example of a voltage and current waveforms of a linear load is shown in Figure 1.1.
A load is considered “non-linear” if its impedance changes with the applied voltage. Due to this changing
impedance, the current drawn by the non-linear load is also non-linear i.e., non-sinusoidal in nature, even
when it is connected to a sinusoidal voltage source (for example computers, variable frequency drives,
discharge lighting etc.). An example of a voltage and current waveforms of a non-linear load is shown in
Figure 1.2.
These non-sinusoidal currents generate harmonic currents that interact with the impedance of the power
distribution system, leading to non-linear voltage drops and resulting voltage distortion. This distortion
can adversely impact both the distribution system equipment and the connected loads, compromising
performance and efficiency.
IEEE 519-2022 defines harmonics as sinusoidal components of order greater than one of the Fourier
series of a periodic quantity. For example, in a 60 Hz system, the harmonic order 3 (also known as the
“third harmonic”), is 180 Hz.

different purpose. The PWM voltage waveform produced by a VFD has very fast rise times and can create

3. Improved Input Power Factor and Reduced Line Stress
While the primary reasons to use line reactors are typically harmonics and surge protection, an additional
benefit is a slight improvement in input power factor and reduction of line-current peaks that stress
upstream components. Drives without reactors have a displacement power factor near unity (because the
rectifier draws current in phase with voltage when it conducts), but the distortion of the waveform results in
a lower true power factor (often around 0.6–0.7 for small drives). By filtering the waveform, reactors cause
the drive to draw current over a longer portion of each cycle rather than sharp pulses at the peaks . This
means the fundamental component of current is closer to the total current. Users have noted that adding a
5% reactor can raise the power factor into the 0.90+ range for many drives .

verdict.summary:
Assumptions and method

- System: three-phase, 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz feeder.
- Load: 75 kVA at 0.8 lagging. Load current: I_L = 75000 / (sqrt(3) x 400) = 108.25 A.
- Catalogue x is per-unit reactance on a 100 kVA base at rated voltage. For a 400 V three-phase base, Z_base = V_LL^2 / S_base = 400^2 / 100000 = 1.6 ohm. Reactance X = x x 1.6 ohm.
- Voltage drop through the reactor is taken as the reactor terminal reactance voltage drop, I_L X, with winding resistance negligible. This follows the IEEE C57.16 definition: reactance voltage drop = rated reactance x current. Expressed as a percentage of the 400 V system voltage: %drop = (I_L X) / (400/sqrt(3)) x 100 = 100 x x x (75/100) = 75x. The 0.8 lagging power factor does not change the reactor terminal drop magnitude because R = 0; it would enter only a load-terminal voltage-regulation calculation.

Catalogue screening

All Bay models have rated voltage 400 V >= 380 V, rated frequency 50 Hz >= 50 Hz, and rated current at least 230.9 A >= 108.25 A, so all pass the voltage, frequency, and rated-current constraints. The voltage-drop calculation at the 75 kVA load gives:

| B-320 | 0.055 | 0.088 | 4.125 | No | 4500 |
| B-500 | 0.040 | 0.064 | 3.000 | Yes | 6100 |

The maximum power dissipated in each transistor is one-fifth the maximum power that the push-pull stage can deliver to the load.
Let’s contrast this with Figure 6, which reproduces the power terms of the inductively-loaded Class A configuration.
Figure 6. Supply power (PCC), load power (PL), transistor power (PTran), and power efficiency versus collector current (ic) for an inductively-loaded Class A amplifier.
In a Class A stage, the transistor is always biased on. A constant DC current is drawn from the supply even when no AC signal is applied. As a result, PCC is always constant, and remains non-zero even in the absence of an AC signal. Because the transistor is always biased on, a significant amount of power is wasted in the transistor as heat.
With a Class B amplifier, PCC increases linearly with the collector current. No power is burned in the transistors when the amplitude of the AC signal is very small, leading to a much higher efficiency.

The voltage at node A is in phase with the input, whereas the voltage at node B is 180 degrees out of phase. Vbias is chosen appropriately to bias the transistors just below their turn-on point. With that in mind, let's work through an example.
Example: Choosing the Turns Ratio For Maximum Output Power
Assume that the transistor for the push-pull amplifier in Figure 8 has the following specifications:
Maximum collector current (ic,max) = 1 A.
Maximum collector-emitter breakdown voltage (BVCEO) = 40 V.
Maximum power the transistor can handle without being damaged (PC,max) = 4 W.
Let’s find the appropriate turns ratio for the output transformer to deliver maximum power to a 50 Ω load.
First, we’ll find the voltage and current swing at the collector. To find the corresponding output swings, we’ll scale them by the turns ratio of the transformer. We know that the amplitude of the half-sine wave collector current is limited by the maximum permissible current of the transistor: Ip = ic,max = 1 A. Besides, since the collector voltage swings from 0 to 2VCC, we should choose the supply voltage to be half BVCEO to avoid damaging the transistor.

verdict.summary:
Selection basis
- Catalogue used: T4-42-1.md, Nordline VL voltage-source inverters only.
- Motor: 15 kW shaft output, 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz, PF 0.84, efficiency 0.90.
- Supply: 400 V, 50 Hz.
- 'Covers' is applied strictly as U_min <= 400 V <= U_max, f_min <= 50 Hz <= f_max, P_n >= 15 kW, and I_n >= motor current expressed in the same amplitude convention. No extra service-factor or overload margin is added because the request specifies only 'covers'.
- The catalogue defines I_n as the amplitude of the permissible sinusoidal output current. Therefore the motor RMS line current is converted to peak amplitude before comparison with I_n, or equivalently the RMS motor current is compared with I_n/sqrt(2).

Motor line current
The 15 kW is shaft output, so the input electrical power at rated load is:
P_in = P_out / efficiency = 15000 / 0.90 = 16666.7 W
Motor line current, RMS:
I_L = P_in / (sqrt(3) * U_L * PF) = 16666.7 / (sqrt(3) * 400 * 0.84) = 28.64 A
Motor line current, peak amplitude:
I_L,peak = sqrt(2) * 28.64 = 40.50 A
Using 25.8 A by omitting efficiency would be the shaft-power-equivalent current, not the motor input line current; efficiency is given and must be included.

Catalogue screen
All four VL units have U_min = 380 V, U_max = 480 V, so all cover the 400 V supply. All have f_min = 0 Hz and f_max = 60 Hz, so all cover 50 Hz. All have P_n >= 15 kW. The current test discriminates:

quotes.whole:
A retrofit reactor is ordered against measured conditions, not the original drawings, and five checks avoid most surprises.
1. Measure the drive’s actual input current (line reactor) or the motor’s running current (load reactor) at full process load with a true-RMS meter, and select from the current rather than the horsepower; a 40 HP drive running a 25 HP load at 208 V is a 3PR-0080 selection, not a 3PR-0130.
2. Confirm the system voltage at the drive terminals, since the part number does not carry it.
3. Look at the drive lineup: whether there is a bypass contactor and where the reactor must sit relative to it, and whether the drive already has a DC choke.
4. Measure the available space and check the panel’s cooling, because a reactor adds a continuous heat source; an enclosed unit outside the panel is often simpler than finding room inside. Dimensions for the selected voltage and impedance are in the Line Reactor catalogue.
5. On a load-side retrofit, record the motor cable length and type and the drive’s carrier frequency, which decide between a load reactor and a Motor Guarding Transient Filter, and plan to re-run the drive’s autotune after installation.

quotes.whole:
Consider a 13.8 kV switchgear bus with 25 kA symmetrical available fault current, feeding a 1,200 A feeder to a downstream lineup rated for 18 kA. A series air core reactor in the feeder must add enough reactance to hold the downstream fault below that rating; neglecting resistance and the downstream cable:
• Source reactance per phase: X_s = 7,967 V / 25,000 A = 0.319 Ω.
• Total reactance needed for 18 kA: X_t = 7,967 / 18,000 = 0.443 Ω.
• Reactor reactance: X_r = 0.443 − 0.319 = 0.124 Ω per phase.
• Inductance at 60 Hz: L = 0.124 / (2π × 60) = 0.33 mH per phase.
The nameplate would state 0.33 mH, 1,200 A continuous, 15 kV class with a matching BIL, and a short-circuit rating of 18 kA symmetrical for the relay clearing time. Reactive power at rated current is 3 × 1,200² × 0.124 = 536 kVAR, and on the feeder’s own base (7,967 V / 1,200 A = 6.64 Ω) it is a 1.9 percent reactor.
Two refinements belong in the real study: motor contribution downstream of the reactor is not limited by it, and the X/R ratio at the reactor terminals rises, increasing the DC offset the breaker must interrupt. The Knowledge Hub article Impedance in Transformers explains the per-unit conventions used above.

quotes.whole:
How does a Rex air core reactor behave at 50 Hz compared with 60 Hz, and can one unit serve both?
The product page lists 60 Hz standard with 50/60 Hz optional. Inductance is a property of coil geometry and does not change with frequency, so a Rex air core reactor rated in millihenries has the same inductance at either frequency. Everything derived from inductance does change.
Reactance scales directly with frequency, X = 2πfL, so the same coil presents five-sixths of its 60 Hz reactance at 50 Hz. A current-limiting reactor designed for 60 Hz lets through about 20 percent more fault current at 50 Hz, and a filter reactor that is 7 percent detuned at 60 Hz is 5.8 percent detuned at 50 Hz, moving the tuning order from 3.78 to 4.14 relative to the new fundamental. The kVAR absorbed by a shunt reactor at rated voltage rises by 20 percent at 50 Hz because the current rises.
There is no core to overheat, so unlike a transformer an air core reactor is not damaged by operation at the lower frequency; it simply does not deliver the same reactance.

quotes.whole:
Should I specify a Rex air core reactor in millihenries, percent reactance or kVAR?
All three describe the same coil, but each is complete only with a stated base. The clearest specification for a Rex air core reactor gives the inductance in millihenries, the rated continuous current, the system voltage and the frequency. Inductance needs no base.
Percent reactance is convenient for current-limiting reactors because fault studies work in per-unit, but it must state its base. A “5 percent reactor” on a 1,200 A, 13.8 kV feeder base is 0.33 Ω; the same 5 percent on a 20 MVA transformer base at 13.8 kV is 0.48 Ω. Always give the current or MVA base alongside the percentage.
kVAR describes the reactive power at rated current, 3 × I² × X for a three-phase set, and is the natural rating for shunt reactors, which is why the product page expresses capacity as 10,000 kVAR. For a series or filter reactor, kVAR alone does not define the coil, because different current and inductance combinations give the same kVAR.

## Selection calculation

**Basis.** Three-phase, 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz. The catalogue kVA/current pairs confirm three-phase ratings (e.g. B-160: 160,000/(√3·400) = 230.9 A), so the load current is

I_L = 75,000/(√3·400) = 108.25 A.

The load power factor (0.8 lagging) fixes the current angle but does not change the magnitude of the voltage across a purely reactive series element. Using the IEEE/C57 definition of reactance voltage drop (the component in quadrature with current), the reactor drop is I_L·X. Winding resistance is negligible per the catalogue.

**Per-unit conversion.** The catalogue x is on a 100 kVA base at 400 V:

Z_b = V_LL²/S_b = 400²/100,000 = 1.6 Ω
X = x·Z_b
Drop (%) = (I_L·X / (400/√3))·100 = (√3·I_L·X/400)·100 = x·(75/100)·100 = 75x %.

**Candidate check.**

| Model | X (Ω) | I_L·X (V/phase) | Drop (%) | Rated current (A) | Rated V / f | Price (EUR) | Meets all? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|
| B-160 | 0.128 | 13.86 | 6.000 | 230.9 | 400 V / 50 Hz | 2000 | No — drop |
| B-200 | 0.120 | 12.99 | 5.625 | 288.7 | 400 V / 50 Hz | 2800 | No — drop |
| B-320 | 0.088 | 9.53 | 4.125 | 461.9 | 400 V / 50 Hz | 4500 | No — drop |
| B-500 | 0.064 | 6.93 | 3.000 | 721.7 | 400 V / 50 Hz | 6100 | Yes |

All models satisfy rated voltage (400 V ≥ 380 V), rated frequency (50 Hz ≥ 50 Hz), and rated current (minimum 230.9 A ≥ 108.25 A). The 3.0% voltage-drop limit eliminates B-160, B-200 and B-320. B-500 is the only compliant model, at exactly 3.000% (equality is allowed by “shall not exceed 3.0%”), so it is the cheapest compliant selection. Price: EUR 6,100.

**Convention note.** If “voltage drop” were instead intended as the load-terminal voltage-regulation approximation ΔV/V ≈ x(S_L/S_b)sinφ, B-320 would appear compliant and cheaper. That is a different quantity from the reactor’s reactance voltage drop; the catalogue gives x and the IEEE/C57 reactance voltage drop is I·X, which is the convention used here.

This is the three-phase power equation, kW = V × I × PF × √3 ÷ 1,000, solved for current [1]. A line-to-neutral voltage is multiplied by √3 first to give the line-to-line voltage [2], so 230 V line-to-neutral is treated as 398.4 V.
Current from power
With kW or W, the main formula applies directly. A 10 kW heater has a power factor of 1 and draws 12.03 A at 480 V, 14.43 A at 400 V and 27.76 A at 208 V.

kW = hp × 0.7457 ÷ η [1]
Motor horsepower is output power, so it is converted to input kW with the efficiency η as a decimal and then put through the main formula. A 50 hp motor at 90% efficiency takes 41.43 kW, which is 58.62 A at 480 V and a power factor of 0.85.
Power from current
kVA = √3 × V × I ÷ 1,000
Real power is then kW = kVA × PF, and reactive power is kVA × √(1 − PF²). A line current of 100 A at 480 V is 83.14 kVA. At a power factor of 0.85 that is 70.67 kW and 43.80 kvar.
Limits of This Estimate
The formulas are for a balanced load with sine-wave voltage and current. Unequal phase loads and harmonic currents are not modelled.
The 0.85 power factor and 90% motor efficiency are starting values. The figures on the motor nameplate give a closer result.
The result is the running current. It does not size breakers, conductors or motor protection, which follow the electrical code.

quotes.whole:
Mechanical (shaft) power from torque and speed: P(kW) = T × N / 9550, where T is torque in Nm and N is speed in rpm.
Electrical input power for a three-phase motor: P(kW) = √3 × V × I × PF / 1000, where V is line voltage, I is line current and PF is power factor.
The constant 9550 bundles the unit conversions (it is 60,000 / 2π). Memorise it — it turns Nm and rpm straight into kW.
Power from torque and speed
When you know the load torque and the running speed, mechanical power is direct. Say a mixer needs 120 Nm at 1450 rpm:
P = T × N / 9550
P = 120 × 1450 / 9550 = 18.2 kW at the shaft. That is the power the load demands; the motor must deliver at least this on its output shaft.
If your speed is in rad/s rather than rpm, use the cleaner form P(W) = T(Nm) × ω(rad/s). The 9550 version simply saves you converting rpm every time.
Electrical input power and current
The nameplate kW is shaft output. The motor draws more than that from the supply because of losses, so:
Input power = output power / efficiency. A 18.5 kW motor at 91% efficiency draws 18.5 / 0.91 = 20.3 kW electrical input.
To find the running current, rearrange the three-phase formula:
I = P(input, W) / (√3 × V × PF)

Add a service factor of 15–25% — not 100%.
Pick the next standard frame up, then check it runs near 75–100% load.
A motor loaded to 75–95% of rating is in its efficiency and power-factor sweet spot. For pump and fan drives, remember the affinity laws — power rises with the cube of speed, so a small speed increase is a big power increase. If energy cost is the target, our OEE guide and cycle time guide help connect motor loading to real output.
Watch the part-load power factor
Power factor on an induction motor falls from ~0.86 at full load to ~0.5 at quarter load. An oversized motor not only wastes real power, it drags your plant power factor down and can attract a utility penalty. Size to the load, not to "just in case".
Common motor calculation mistakes
Confusing input and output. Nameplate kW is shaft output; supply draw is higher by the efficiency loss.
Forgetting √3. The 1.732 factor is mandatory for three-phase — leaving it out understates power by 42%.
Ignoring drive losses. Gearboxes, belts and couplings each take a few percent.
Sizing on running power only. Starting torque for high-inertia or loaded starts can need a larger frame.

quotes.whole:
In electrical systems, voltage is the force required to move electrons. Current is the rate of the flow of charge per second through a material to which a specific voltage is applied. By taking the voltage and multiplying it by the associated current, the power can be determined.
P = V * I where power (P) is in watts, voltage (V) is in volts and current (I) is in amperes
A watt (W) is a unit of power defined as one Joule per second. For a DC source the calculation is simply the voltage times the current: W = V x A. However, determining the power in watts for an AC source must include the power factor (PF), so W = V x A x PF for AC systems.
The power factor is a unitless ratio ranging from -1 to 1, and represents the amount of real power performing work at a load. For power factors less than unity, which is almost always the case, there will be losses in real power. This is because the voltage and current of an AC circuit are sinusoidal in nature, with the amplitude of the current and voltage of an AC circuit constantly shifting and not typically in perfect alignment.

quotes.whole:
Three-wire and four-wire power measurements
It's important to recognize that power will read the same regardless if it's measured in a three-phase three-wire or a three-phase four-wire method. However, using a three-phase four-wire connection, the voltage values being measured are phase voltages from line-to-neutral.
Figure 6 is a screen shot from a power analyzer that shows how similar the power and power factor readings are for a PWM drive operating a motor, comparing a three-phase three-wire 500 Hz filtered input against a three-phase four-wire floating neutral input.
An alternative solution uses a delta measurement function that is found in Yokogawa power analyzers. The delta measurement function uses instantaneous line-to-line voltage and phase current measurements to derive a true line-to-neutral voltage, even if the phases are unbalanced. A vector amplitude calculation inside the processor makes this possible. This function also provides the phase power measurements on the three-wire circuit. The delta measurement solution also provides the neutral current.

A more integrated approach is depicted in Figure 6. With this configuration, the speed and torque signal outputs from the sensor instrumentation are connected directly to power analyzer speed and torque inputs. This offers the big advantage of enabling electrical and mechanical power measurements to be evaluated simultaneously, and efficiency calculations to be performed continuously.
Motor, drive, and system efficiency
Inverter efficiency in its simplest form is calculated as output power divided by input power, and represented as a percentage. One method used to measure input and output power is simply to connect power meters on the input and output, with the readings of the two meters used to calculate efficiency.
A more comprehensive method is to use a multiple input power analyzer to measure input and output simultaneously as shown in Figure 1. This results in a more accurate efficiency calculation as it uses a single power analyzer to eliminate potential errors caused by time skew measurements.
With the internal math calculations provided by the analyzer, a very simple, menu-driven computation can be set up to take calculate the drive loss and drive efficiency.

verdict.summary:
SELECTION OF A NORDLINE VL INVERTER FOR A 15 kW, 400 V, 50 Hz INDUCTION MOTOR

1. MOTOR LINE CURRENT
Given: shaft output P = 15 kW, line-to-line voltage U = 400 V, frequency 50 Hz, power factor cos φ = 0.84, efficiency η = 0.90.
The nameplate kW of an induction motor is mechanical shaft output, so the electrical input power is
  P_in = P / η = 15 / 0.90 = 16.667 kW
and the line current (RMS, balanced, sinusoidal) is
  I = P_in / (√3 · U · cos φ) = 16666.7 / (1.7320508 × 400 × 0.84)
    = 16666.7 / 581.969 = 28.64 A
Single-step form: I = P / (√3 · U · cos φ · η) = 15000 / (1.7320508 × 400 × 0.84 × 0.90) = 15000 / 523.772 = 28.64 A.
Cross-check via apparent power: S = P_in / cos φ = 16.667 / 0.84 = 19.841 kVA; I = S / (√3 · U) = 19841 / 692.82 = 28.64 A. Agrees.
Result: motor line current I = 28.64 A (28.6 A to 1 d.p.).

2. CANDIDATE FILTERING AGAINST THE VL CATALOGUE (T4-42-1.md only)
Criteria (all endpoints inclusive):
  (a) U_min ≤ 400 V ≤ U_max
  (b) f_min ≤ 50 Hz ≤ f_max
  (c) P_n ≥ 15 kW
  (d) I_n ≥ 28.64 A
  (e) lowest price among those passing (a)–(d).

|-------|----------|-------------------|----------|-------------------|----------|-----------------|---------|--------------------|-------------|
| VL-25 | 380–480 V | yes | 0–60 Hz | yes | 18   | yes | 33 | yes (margin 4.36 A) | 410 |
| VL-36 | 380–480 V | yes | 0–60 Hz | yes | 18.5 | yes | 38 | yes (margin 9.36 A) | 520 |
| VL-42 | 380–480 V | yes | 0–60 Hz | yes | 22   | yes | 46 | yes (margin 17.36 A) | 640 |
| VL-60 | 380–480 V | yes | 0–60 Hz | yes | 30   | yes | 62 | yes (margin 33.36 A) | 890 |

All four models pass the voltage, frequency, power and current screens, so the decision is made by price alone. The lowest-price qualifying unit is VL-25 at 410 EUR (410 < 520 < 640 < 890).

3. SELECTED UNIT — CHECKS
  Model: Nordline VL-25, 410 EUR, 5.2 kg.
  Supply: 400 V lies inside 380–480 V (margin 20 V below, 80 V above the window edges).
  Output frequency: 50 Hz lies inside 0–60 Hz.
  Rated power: P_n = 18 kW ≥ 15 kW (20 % power headroom).
  Output current: I_n = 33 A ≥ 28.64 A. Headroom = 33 − 28.64 = 4.36 A; motor draws 86.8 % of I_n (13.2 % margin).

4. NOTES / SENSITIVITY
  a) I_n definition. The catalogue states I_n is the amplitude of the permissible sinusoidal output current. This selection compares the motor RMS line current (28.64 A) directly with I_n (33 A), as the request specifies a direct comparison and the catalogue publishes only I_n. If 'amplitude' were instead read strictly as a peak value, the permissible RMS would be I_n/√2 (VL-25: 23.3 A, VL-36: 26.9 A, VL-42: 32.5 A, VL-60: 43.8 A), VL-25 and VL-36 would fail, and the lowest-price qualifying unit would become VL-42 at 640 EUR. That alternative should be confirmed with Nordline before ordering if the peak interpretation is intended.
  b) No derating applied: catalogue values are used at face value (no ambient-temperature, altitude or switching-frequency derating), per the stated assumption. Confirm the enclosure ambient and any long-motor-cable derating before release.
  c) The motor is assumed to run at full rated load on a 400 V supply at its nameplate voltage, i.e. the worst-case steady-state current. Starting/inrush is handled by the inverter's current limit and is not part of this steady-state screen; overload capability (e.g. 150 % for 60 s) is not given in the VL catalogue and is not claimed here.
  d) Rounding: currents reported to 2 d.p. (28.64 A); the selection is insensitive to rounding since the smallest margin is 4.36 A.

Look down the resistance column and it falls by more than two orders of magnitude from the smallest to the largest size; look down the reactance column and it barely moves, hovering near 0.08 Ω/km0.08 Ω/km throughout. How does conductor voltage drop over run differ from cable ampacity sizing?
Conductor thermal ampacity rating limits continuous current carrying capacity before insulation sustains damage, whereas voltage drop governs delivered terminal voltage over run distance. Two cables sharing identical ampacity can experience completely different voltage drops depending on length, material resistivity, operating temperature, and load power factor over long routes.
When should engineers not use basic conductor upsizing to solve conductor voltage drop over run?
Reactance-dominated large feeder circuits fee
quotes.whole:
How does conductor voltage drop over run differ from cable ampacity sizing?
Conductor thermal ampacity rating limits continuous current carrying capacity before insulation sustains damage, whereas voltage drop governs delivered terminal voltage over run distance. Two cables sharing identical ampacity can experience completely different voltage drops depending on length, material resistivity, operating temperature, and load power factor over long routes.
When should engineers not use basic conductor upsizing to solve conductor voltage drop over run?
Reactance-dominated large feeder circuits feeding low power factor loads render upsizing copper ineffective. Because doubling conductor cross-sectional area halves resistance while inductive reactance barely changes from 0.08 ohms per kilometre, engineers should apply power factor correction, split into parallel runs, or raise the distribution voltage instead of merely adding copper.

# Series reactor selection — Lumenford Bay series, 400 V / 50 Hz feeder

## 1. Duty

| Quantity | Value | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Load apparent power | 75 kVA | given |
| Load power factor | 0.8 lagging (sinφ = 0.6) | given |
| Feeder voltage | 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz | given |
| Load current | 108.25 A | I = S/(√3·V_LL) = 75,000/(1.732051·400) |

I = 75,000 / 692.82 = **108.25 A** (≈108.3 A). Power factor does not affect this current; it enters only the voltage-drop calculation below.

## 2. Catalogue data converted to ohms

The catalogue defines x as per-unit reactance on a 100 kVA base at rated voltage (400 V).

Z_base = V²/S_base = 400² / 100,000 = **1.6 Ω**, therefore X = 1.6·x Ω per phase. Winding resistance is stated negligible (R = 0), so Z = jX.

| Model | V rated (V) | f rated (Hz) | I rated (A) | S rated (kVA) | x (pu) | X (Ω) | Price (EUR) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| B-160 | 400 | 50 | 230.9 | 160 | 0.080 | 0.128 | 2,000 |
| B-200 | 400 | 50 | 288.7 | 200 | 0.075 | 0.120 | 2,800 |
| B-320 | 400 | 50 | 461.9 | 320 | 0.055 | 0.088 | 4,500 |
| B-500 | 400 | 50 | 721.7 | 500 | 0.040 | 0.064 | 6,100 |

## 3. Voltage-drop calculation

**Convention used.** The drop that matters to the load is the component of the reactor drop in phase with the load voltage. With R = 0 the standard three-phase feeder expression ΔV% = √3·I·(R cosφ + X sinφ)/V_LL × 100 collapses to:

ΔV% = √3 · I · X · sinφ / 400 × 100 = I · X · 0.6 / 230.94 × 100

Equivalently, in per-unit terms on the 100 kVA / 400 V base: ΔV(pu) = (S_load/S_base)·x·sinφ = 0.75·x·0.6. Both forms give identical answers; the 400 V line-to-line base is used for the percentage (line-to-neutral base would give the same percentage — the √3 cancels consistently).

Worked example, B-320: X = 0.088 Ω; I·X = 108.25 × 0.088 = 9.526 V per phase (reactor terminal voltage); in-phase component = 9.526 × 0.6 = 5.716 V; 5.716 / 230.94 = 0.02475 → **2.475 %**. Per-unit check: 0.75 × 0.055 × 0.6 = 0.02475 ✓.

| Model | X (Ω) | I·X (V/ph) | In-phase drop I·X·sinφ (V/ph) | ΔV (%) | ≤ 3.0 %? |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| B-160 | 0.128 | 13.856 | 8.314 | 3.600 | No |
| B-200 | 0.120 | 12.990 | 7.794 | 3.375 | No |
| B-320 | 0.088 | 9.526 | 5.716 | 2.475 | Yes |
| B-500 | 0.064 | 6.928 | 4.157 | 1.800 | Yes |

**Exact phasor cross-check** (V_s = V_r + jX·I with V_r = 230.94∠0 V, I = 108.25∠−36.87° A): B-320 → |V_s| = 236.78 V, regulation 2.53 %; B-200 → 3.47 %; B-160 → 3.71 %. Same pass/fail split, same selection — the result does not depend on using the approximate or the exact regulation formula.

**Convention note (for transparency).** If "voltage drop through the reactor" were instead read as the full terminal voltage across the reactor, I·X (no sinφ), the numbers become 6.00 % / 5.625 % / 4.125 % / 3.00 %; B-320 would then fail and B-500 would be the cheapest compliant unit at exactly 3.00 % (6,100 EUR). That reading is rejected here because (a) the request supplies the 0.8 lagging power factor, which is only meaningful if the reactive current component I·sinφ is intended, and (b) the standard feeder-drop formulation and the reference material both attribute the governing drop to the reactive component of load current. The selection below is made on that basis.

## 4. Constraint screening

| Model | I rated ≥ 108.25 A? | V rated ≥ 380 V? | f rated ≥ 50 Hz? | ΔV ≤ 3.0 %? | Compliant? | Price (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| B-160 | Yes (230.9 A) | Yes (400 V) | Yes (50 Hz) | No (3.60 %) | **No** | 2,000 |
| B-200 | Yes (288.7 A) | Yes (400 V) | Yes (50 Hz) | No (3.38 %) | **No** | 2,800 |
| B-320 | Yes (461.9 A) | Yes (400 V) | Yes (50 Hz) | Yes (2.48 %) | **Yes** | 4,500 |
| B-500 | Yes (721.7 A) | Yes (400 V) | Yes (50 Hz) | Yes (1.80 %) | **Yes** | 6,100 |

All four catalogue entries share the 400 V / 50 Hz rating, so the voltage and frequency constraints do not discriminate. The current constraint is met by every model — the 108.25 A load is well below even the B-160's 230.9 A. The drop limit is the binding constraint: it eliminates the two cheapest models (B-160 and B-200), so price ranking applies only to B-320 and B-500.

**Selection:** lowest price among compliant models → **B-320, 4,500 EUR**. Voltage drop 2.475 % (0.53 percentage points of margin under the 3.0 % limit); rated current 461.9 A against a 108.25 A load (4.27× margin, a consequence of the drop limit rather than of ampacity); rated voltage 400 V ≥ 380 V; rated frequency 50 Hz ≥ 50 Hz; sourced exclusively from the Lumenford Bay series catalogue.

| Reactor | Voltage drop (%) | Current (A) | Price (EUR) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
